newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW - UK Sept PMI.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - UK Sept PMI.

text.p: Following is a list of reactions to UK Sept PMI data published at 0830 GMT.
** THE FIGURES SHOWED THE INDEX ROSE TO 53.4, THE HIGEST LEVEL FOR 17 MONTHS
** MARKET FORECASTS WERE FOR A SMALLER INCREASE TO 51.9

"It looks like manufacturing has turned the corner. The service sector has been booming for some time and manufacturing has been very dormant but now at least things seem to getting better and you're gping to see output increasing.

"Clearly if you add on the fact that three quarters of the economy is doing very well and the one quareter that was doing very poorly is now doing a bit better, it does add up to the fact there is going to be more inflationary pressure at the end of the year or early next year than we thought formerly."

"The UK purchasing managers index is strong, but not inflationary. Overall breakdown is positive with very strong orders and output. However, key price index still subdued at 44, well below the key 50 mark, and so should bode well for upcoming PPIs. The report again shows that much of the pick-up in activity has to do with the consumer sector, but a better balance of growth now seen with gains in investment goods too. Employment about the only disappointing area. Overall, it again argues against any more rate cuts but at the same time, does not in itself call for a rate hike."
Marian Bell, Royal Bank of Scotland

"The survey is very strong...manufacturing has turned the corner. We were forecasting a pick-up although not a number as high as this, but we're not surprised as we're very bullish about the economy and growth. The prices index itself is not showing anything to be particularly worried about, there are worries for inflation stemming more generally from the pace of growth in the economy."

"The report confirms that the manufacturing sector is continuing to recover. The bits that stand out are the increases in output and new orders. Coupled with the fall in stocks we saw in the second quarter, it seems the prospects for manufacturing are brighter than had been thought. The prices index is picking up and with relatively firm oil prices and domestic demand, I would not expect the subdued run of PPI figures to continue into next year. Fiscal policy will be dictated by political considerations. We're bound to see some tax cuts, albeit matched with spending cuts.

Monetary policy is a puzzle. The recent strong data have raised the prospect of a rate rise before the election. Previously, that was unthinkable. Clarke may be hard pushed not to raise rates but the economic evidence would have to be irrefutable for him to move. There will be immense weight of political pressure against it."
